A small church on the Quirinal Hill in Rome, the first building Francesco Borromini designed on his own, and a founding work of Baroque architecture. It was built for the Spanish Trinitarians, an order devoted to freeing Christians held as slaves, at the crossroads called the Four Fountains, where a fountain stands on each corner. Borromini, until then an assistant to Carlo Maderno at St Peter's, offered to work for nothing to start his own career. He took the job in 1634 with the backing of Cardinal Francesco Barberini, built the friars' rooms and the cloister first, and raised the church in 1638 to 1641; it was dedicated to Saint Charles Borromeo in 1646.

The site was cramped, and the church is tiny, about 66 by 39 feet. Borromini based the plan on geometric figures rather than on the proportions of the human body, as most architects of the time did. Sixteen columns in groups of four carry an entablature that bends in and out, so the walls seem to ripple. Above, pendentives lead up to an oval dome lined with deep coffers of octagons, crosses and hexagons that shrink as they rise, lit by windows hidden from below, so the light is brightest at the lantern and fades toward the floor.

The cloister next door is a long rectangle with its corners cut, so it can also be read as a stretched octagon. The curving front, concave and convex in turn, was planned early but built only at the end of Borromini's life; he died in 1667, and his nephew Bernardo finished it by 1682. Down the same street stands Sant'Andrea al Quirinale, the oval church of Borromini's rival Bernini.
